name: Sara Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Sara, 43, with a music bachelor’s. I play keyboard for a wedding band and a church, make simple piano guides so singers can rehearse at home, and teach seven pupils in the afternoon. I have years of bookings and am an ordinary dependable player, not the one called for a big solo. I love the moment a nervous bride walks in on time; I dislike a client treating a guide recording as free because it is short.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household relying on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner manages a building-supply shop, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage, but my music pay is high for this line of work and about eight months of expenses are saved. There are plenty of teaching and playing posts nearby, though I would still need a posted opening. I have never used an AI tool and would rather keep a pencil by the keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the wedding band that a faster invoice is fine if the player still earns the agreed fee. The singers still need someone who can follow a breath at the keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have eight months saved and my partner’s shop wage is steady. One delayed wedding cheque would be inconvenient, but the mortgage would be paid this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the church service, booked weddings and seven pupils this winter. I would ask couples to put deposits and cancellation terms in writing before reserving a Saturday, then save part of each cleared wedding fee after the mortgage is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our work in a small-change world. A late deposit is a nuisance, not a reason to take food money from the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a cancelled Saturday cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wedding can cover several weeks of music lessons for our own children. I would ask for a cancellation date in the contract before promising that money to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use software to write a guide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI for a piano guide. I can play a line slowly and hear when a singer needs a different note.

say: I would accept faster **invoices** while insisting on the agreed player fee.
I would ask couples for **written deposits** before saving a Saturday.
think: Eight months of **savings** and the shop wage cover a late cheque.
A cancelled **wedding fee** still matters to the children’s music costs.
do: Keep **church, weddings and pupils** this winter.
Get **deposits and cancellation terms** in writing; save part of cleared wedding fees after the mortgage.
feel: I feel **calm** because existing bookings and savings cover ordinary delays.
S0.quote: A late deposit is a nuisance, not a reason to take food money from the children.
fieldNote: Her **high pay**, partner’s regular shop wage and eight-month reserve support a calm baseline despite occasional delayed wedding deposits.
She **never uses AI** and seeks written terms directly from wedding clients.

steps.text: Keep paid church service, booked weddings and seven pupils this winter
Get wedding deposits and cancellation terms in writing before reserving Saturdays
Save part of each cleared wedding fee after mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band that a generated practice guide could take a small paid job before anyone replaces a live keyboard. I would ask each choir for a price and permission before it reuses one of my recordings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The home-practice guides are about a quarter of my music income. If choirs stop buying them, we can draw on savings, but I would lose a real part of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d list which guide orders are paid and ask choir directors for written reuse terms. In the first year, if guide orders fall, I’d stop renting the extra recording keyboard on days with no paid session and keep the church, weddings and pupils while they pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing a quarter of my own income, even with savings. I can work harder at live bookings, but I cannot make a choir buy a guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which guide is first at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first would be a slow piano part for singers learning a new hymn at home. A generated guide could arrive before a robot can sit at my keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join a campaign about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would rather show the choir an invoice and ask for a fair fee face to face. If that fails, I would look for paid playing instead of borrowing for new software.

I would tell the band that **generated guides** reach paid recordings first.
think: Guide orders make about **one quarter** of my music pay.
Our **reserve** gives time, but cannot replace that income forever.
do: List **paid guide orders** and request reuse terms this month.
Stop **keyboard rental** on empty days if guides fall; keep paid church, weddings and pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a likely loss of my own guide fees.
S1.quote: I can work harder at live bookings, but I cannot make a choir buy a guide.
fieldNote: Her threatened **guide fees** are a quarter of music income despite strong savings.
She asks **choir directors directly** for terms and cuts empty equipment rental.

steps.text: Ask choir directors for written recording reuse terms this month
Stop extra recording-keyboard rental on empty days if paid guides fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AGI in 2028 could make the singers’ piano guides cheaply, while robots able to play hands-on music arrive around 2031. I would ask the wedding band for its paid dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most guide orders to stop by 2028, taking a quarter of my pay. A live wedding may last longer, but a full calendar is not a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d get written wedding and church dates and keep seven pupils. In the first year after AGI arrives, if guide orders stop, I’d end the rented keyboard at renewal and apply for an advertised music-school keyboard post only if the school accepts my degree and experience and the written net wage covers travel and school pickup; I’d keep current bookings until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about that lost quarter, not desperate. Eight months saved lets us check the pay before moving the children’s pickup routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the school rather than another wedding band?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school could give regular paid hours, but I would ask to see the timetable and preparation rate in writing. A vacancy alone is not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a relative cover pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister could collect the children on some days, if she is free. I would confirm the actual week before promising a school an afternoon.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot players around 2031.
I would ask for **written live dates** before counting future weddings.
think: I expect **guide fees** worth a quarter of pay to stop.
A live **wedding calendar** is not guaranteed income.
do: Keep **seven pupils** and live bookings until signed school offer; confirm paid dates before 2028.
End **keyboard rental** at renewal if 2028 guide orders stop.
Seek a **posted school job** if guides stop: accepted credentials, written preparation rate and viable net-after-travel pay with pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a quarter of pay despite savings.
S2.quote: A live wedding may last longer, but a full calendar is not a contract.
fieldNote: The **2028 guide loss** comes before hands-on robot players around 2031.
A school move needs **accepted credentials**, written pay, pickup and a signed offer before leaving current work.

steps.text: Keep paid weddings, church and seven pupils until signed school offer
End recording-keyboard rental at renewal if 2028 guide orders stop
Seek advertised school post if 2028 guides stop, credentials accepted, written net wage covers travel/pickup
Check school timetable and preparation rate in writing before accepting school offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the church that five years lets us see whether adults will pay to learn simple songs together. Thinking AGI reaches guide recordings around 2031, and capable robot keyboard players follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An independent evening singing circle could replace some guide fees, but friendship does not pay my teaching hours. I would not take money out of the mortgage reserve for a hall deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d ask the independent parish hall for a room without a deposit and invite ten adults to prepay for four evening sessions. I’d start only if those fees cover my teaching and preparation time and my partner confirms school pickup; in the first year after 2031 I’d repeat only if ten still pay enough for my time, the room stays free and pickup remains covered, while keeping paid church and wedding dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about likely guide losses, though the extra years let me test a class. A full hall without a teaching fee would be charity with a mortgage attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you cancel the circle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If only seven pay or the hall wants a deposit, I would return their money and keep my existing pupils. I would not borrow against the house for a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would someone else help with the singers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach this small group myself and use songs I already know. If I needed another player, I would ask whether ten payments also cover their fee before inviting them.

say: I would explain that **2031 thinking AGI** precedes robot players around 2034.
I would offer a **paid circle** only if real adults prepay.
think: Ten prepaid adults might replace **guide fees** if teaching and preparation are paid.
I would not spend the **mortgage reserve** on a room deposit.
do: Ask the parish hall for a **free room** next spring; start only if ten prepay teaching and preparation and pickup is covered.
Repeat the **circle** after 2031 only with ten payments covering time, free room and pickup; keep paid church and wedding dates.
Invite an **extra player** only if needed and ten registrations cover their fee.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely guide loss while testing a paid class.
S3.quote: A full hall without a teaching fee would be charity with a mortgage attached.
fieldNote: Her **independent circle** depends on a free room, ten prepayments covering her time and a pickup plan.

Keep paid church and wedding dates while booked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that a decade gives us time to learn an instrument and ask what the work pays. Thinking AGI arrives around 2036, with robot keyboard players around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still have church and wedding dates, but I cannot promise them forever. The mortgage, our eight-month reserve and my partner’s pay make the next few years steady enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep the seven pupils and booked services, and save part of each cleared guide fee after the mortgage and food are paid. Over the decade I’d run the evening circle only with a free room, ten prepayments covering teaching and preparation, and pickup covered; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep it only while those payments cover my work and seek an advertised school post if live bookings end, with accepted credentials and written net pay covering travel and pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about music a decade out, but our present bills are covered. I can ask for a fair fee without pretending we are already out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new keyboard to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would repair the present one while it plays well. I would save a cleared guide fee, not spend a promised fee on equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the church job for a school post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a written school offer shows paid hours that beat travel and pickup costs. I would keep the current services until that offer is signed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide fees could end before I see a school offer. Written wedding dates, a school vacancy with a net wage that covers pickup, and ten paying adults for a class would help. My family can use savings for a gap, but a full room on a poster is no wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays when the same piano guide is used for another season. A choir can reuse one piano guide for a second season, but my first fee paid for only one.

headlineQuote: A choir can reuse one piano guide for a second season, but my first fee paid for only one.
portrait: Sara is a **43-year-old keyboardist** with a music bachelor’s, wedding and church work, guide recordings and seven pupils.
Her **higher pay**, shop-manager partner, mortgage and eight-month reserve support two school-age children.
She **never uses AI** and relies on direct contracts, pencil marks and paid live bookings.
Fast AGI threatens **guide fees** before robot players, so she tests a prepaid independent circle and checks real school openings.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could end guide income before she receives a workable school offer.
whatWouldHelp: Written **wedding dates** and an advertised school role with net pay covering pickup would help.
Ten **prepaid adults** could support a class without using the mortgage reserve.
